transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-16 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Mateo Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Park (CTO, Silverpine), Marcus Li (SRE), Ana Gomez (Regulatory), Samir Patel (Eng Lead)
Shared links: Redwood private runbook (will be shared), HW mapping sheet (pending), air-gapped update example bundle (referenced)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on air-gapped/on-prem update process, hardware constraints and compatibility, validation and audit trails. Customer is evaluating Redwood Private for regulated diagnostics inference inside their ISO-certified data center. Key blockers: zero-internet update process, cert/key rotation in sealed environments, and patch window constraints for medical device workloads.

Topics:
- Offline update mechanics (bundle format, signing, transport)
- Hardware mapping (supported GPUs, fallback CPU paths, quantization tradeoffs)
- Ops & patch windows / maintenance cadence
- Security controls: KMS/HSM, audit logs, RBAC, SSO in disconnected mode
- Validation and regression checks for model updates

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, and with me is Priya and Mateo, our solutions folks. Could you do quick intros?
[00:10] Dr. Park: Sure, I'm Elena Park, CTO at Silverpine. We're building inference for on-prem diagnostic scoring pipelines, very regulated environment.
[00:17] Marcus: Marcus Li, SRE, I run the private datacenter ops and patch windows for the infra that talks to the devices.
[00:22] Ana: Ana Gomez, regulatory, I focus on audit and retention.
[00:25] Samir: Samir Patel, engineering lead on the inference service.
[00:28] Jordan: Great, quick agenda: we want to understand your offline update flow, hardware, how you validate updated models and any compliance constraints. We'll cover what Redwood Private supports today and I'll capture next steps. Sound good?
[00:35] Dr. Park: Yep.

[00:40] Priya: To start, can you describe how you currently update software in the sealed cluster? Do you move bundles on USBs, use controlled bastion hosts, or ship images?
[00:48] Marcus: Right now it's fairly manual — we have signed ISO images that we rsync via a jump host, but the jump host itself is in a DMZ with no outbound internet. For secret rotation we use an HSM appliance but there's no automatic CA renewal from cloud.
[01:02] Priya: Ok, good to know. So key things we hear: signed bundles, jump-host transport, HSM for secrets. Redwood Private supports signed update bundles that can be validated offline — we call them "sealed bundles" in our docs — they include model artifacts, runtime binaries and a manifest. The bundle is signed with customer-managed keys, and validation happens locally.
[01:20] Marcus: Aha. How do you handle key rotations? Our ops team can't have the runtime phone home to Redwood to pull new certs.
[01:27] Mateo: Currently we integrate with on-prem HSMs; for disconnected sites we support manual key import and a rotation helper script that produces a new signed bundle. The certificate itself can be rotated by shipping a rotation artifact in the bundle. There's also a documented process to sign with an offline root CA.
[01:43] Dr. Park: Important: any signing ceremony must be auditable. Ana will require immutable logs showing who signed, when, and the artifact checksum.
[01:50] Ana: Yes, we need chain of custody. Also retention: logs must be kept for 7 years and be exportable for audits.
[01:56] Jordan: We can export signed verification logs from the node; the private control plane (when used in bridge mode in your network) can be configured to ship logs to your SIEM, and on strictly air-gapped installs we provide an offline logs export tool.
[02:06] Samir: Do you store full tokenized cache? We're worried about KV cache persistence across reboots, and if the bundle changes the cache format.
[02:15] Priya: We have a versioned KV cache layout and include migration tooling in the runtime; bundles include a migration manifest. For big model changes we recommend a rolling restart policy and staged cache warmup so you don't regress latency for critical paths.
[02:30] Marcus: How about hardware? We have mixed racks: some A40s, a couple of older V100s, and a subset of machines that are CPU-only for fallback. How tolerant is Redwood to mixed fleets?
[02:40] Mateo: We support model variants and kernel selection at runtime. You can pin a model variant to GPU families, and we have quantized variants for older GPUs / CPU-only paths. The runtime will choose a compatible variant. That said, large changes in model architecture need offline testing — which we recommend as part of the POC.
[03:00] Marcus: Does quantization change outputs in a meaningful way? We have to pass clinical validation post-update.
[03:07] Priya: Quantization can introduce small numeric differences. Redwood Optimize provides diffs and per-prompt evals; in private deployments we can run the same eval harness in your environment and produce a QA report with acceptable thresholds. For clinical workloads you'll likely need to run your own acceptance tests, but we can help with the harness.
[03:24] Dr. Park: Timeline: we need model updates to happen inside our scheduled maintenance windows (Sundays, 02:00-06:00 local) and only after QA sign-off. No emergency auto-updates.
[03:35] Jordan: That's fine — Redwood supports scheduled apply windows for sealed bundles and the rollout policies can be set to manual apply. We also support canary rollouts across pools so you can validate before full rollout.
[03:48] Ana: About audit: do you provide tamper-evident manifests that show which bundle was applied on which node? And do you provide attestations?
[03:56] Mateo: Yes — every node keeps an immutable apply log with the bundle manifest hash and timestamp, and we can produce signed attestations. For truly isolated sites we recommend keeping the attestation keys in your HSM.
[04:09] Marcus: Support model sizes: our largest GPUs are 48GB memory, and some nodes only have 24GB. If I have a 32B parameter model, will Redwood handle sharding or do we need to provide smaller variants?
[04:20] Priya: Redwood runtime supports model sharding across multiple GPUs if the cluster is configured for it; however sharding requires network and interconnect support inside the box. For mixed-memory clusters it's safer to provide a quantized or smaller variant for 24GB nodes. We can advise on model-parallel configs in the POC.
[04:40] Samir: What about offline model validation — we need exact reproducibility so that our QA team can run golden tests. How are bundles versioned?
[04:48] Jordan: Bundles are semantic-versioned and include deterministic build metadata (git commit, build time, checksums). You can pin to a bundle digest. For reproducibility we also support signing the build environment metadata so you can reproduce builds internally.
[05:00] Marcus: Network restrictions: our nodes cannot reach external IPs. If there's a bug requiring a hotfix, what's the remote support story?
[05:08] Jordan: Common pattern: we do remote debug over an approved bastion (ops shares a temporary access key and rbaced session recording), or we ship a hotfix bundle that you apply. For air-gapped, our engineers can provide step-by-step runbook or a signed hotfix artifact. We do not require constant inbound connectivity.
[05:25] Samir: Ok. What about secrets management — KMS/HSM integration for model keys and logs encryption?
[05:31] Mateo: We integrate with on-prem HSMs (PKCS#11) and you can opt to keep keys only in the HSM. We also support envelope encryption and local KMS adapters.
[05:40] Ana: For audits we need key access logs. Will Redwood surface HSM usage or do we need to query the HSM separately?
[05:46] Priya: HSM logs are separate, but Redwood emits events that reference HSM operations (e.g., key id used, operation type). We map those to your audit IDs so you can correlate.
[05:56] Marcus: Performance: what latency overhead does the runtime add compared to a barebones in-house server?
[06:02] Priya: Overhead is usually small — optimized kernels and batching keep latency low. In some cases quantized variants can be faster. We'll run benchmarks during the POC on your HW to show end-to-end latencies.
[06:14] Dr. Park: We also need to understand the upgrade path for the runtime itself — we can't accept any changes to the model interfaces without a change ticket.
[06:20] Jordan: Understood. Runtime upgrades are separate artifacts and can be applied only after manual approval; you can pin runtime versions and we support A/B validation.
[06:30] Marcus: Do you support certificate pinning and local SSO (SAML) federation inside the sealed network?
[06:36] Mateo: For SSO in disconnected mode we support SAML via an internal IdP or by using a local LDAP/AD integration. We also support certificate pinning and provide a cert rotation guide.
[06:46] Ana: Any SOC2/ISO artifacts we can get pre-sale?
[06:50] Jordan: Yes, we can share SOC2 Type II summary and ISO_FAQ redacted artifacts; for Private we have a specific compliance packet. I'll attach it.
[06:58] Samir: Pricing — is there a per-node license or capacity commit?
[07:02] Jordan: Private is typically a platform fee plus support and optionally a license per secured node or committed reserved capacity. We'll send a preliminary commercial outline after this.
[07:11] Dr. Park: One more technical: when applying bundles, can we do a dry-run validation that checks compatibility without applying?
[07:16] Priya: Yes — we have a "validate" command that simulates apply and checks runtime compatibility, disk space, and migration hooks. It returns a validation report.
[07:26] Marcus: Great. About rollback: how fast can we revert if a bundle fails validation post-apply?
[07:31] Mateo: We support atomic apply with rollback. If migration fails, runtime will attempt a rollback using the previous artifact; you'll need the previous bundle available on disk or in your internal artifact store.
[07:43] Ana: For traceability, we need to know who initiated the apply and a signed approval. Can that be captured?
[07:48] Jordan: Yes — apply requires a signed approval token from an authorized approver. That token and the apply event are logged.
[07:56] Samir: Ok, next steps?
[07:58] Jordan: We'll: 1) send the private deployment runbook and the HW mapping spreadsheet, 2) propose a POC plan focused on one rack with representative GPUs, 3) schedule an on-site ops workshop with Mateo.
[08:11] Marcus: We'll export the server SKUs and patch windows and share.
[08:15] Ana: I'll send our audit checklist so you can confirm the artifacts map to our controls.
[08:20] Jordan: Great — we'll follow up with dates. Thanks everyone.

End recap (at ~48 minutes):
- Redwood to share sealed runbook, HW-compat spreadsheet, SOC2 packet, and preliminary pricing.
- Customer to provide SKUs, patch window cadence, and audit checklist.
- Plan: POC on one rack, offline validation harness run, and an on-site ops workshop.

Notes on transcription: audio had small overlaps and one speaker labelled as Speaker 6 in the raw export; names were cleaned where obvious but some acronyms may be transcribed incorrectly (e.g., HSM vendor names).
